[profile]{.eyebrow}

## Research profile

Computational engineer and physicist with a decade of professional experience spanning
scientific research, engineering and accountancy. I hold an integrated Master's degree
in Theoretical Physics and returned to academia after ten years as a Chartered Accountant
to complete an MSc in Medical Engineering. I am now finishing a PhD in the EPSRC Centre
for Doctoral Training in Fluid Dynamics at the University of Leeds.

My PhD involves developing a novel multiscale model to predict friction and lubrication
in total hip replacement bearings, coupling microscale surface physics to macroscale
elastohydrodynamic simulations via the Heterogeneous Multiscale Method. The framework
is implemented using the finite element method in FEniCS and NGSolve and evaluated
through HPC parameter studies. The project is supervised across computer science,
mechanical engineering and industry. Expected completion March 2027.

The intervening decade was spent diagnosing and fixing complex technical and operational
problems in large organisations: identifying the underlying problem, developing and
implementing solutions, delivering to deadlines, and keeping technical and
non-technical stakeholders engaged throughout the process and its outcomes.

[publications]{.eyebrow}

Publications

R. Furze, P. K. Jimack, M. Bryant, M. Al-Hajjar, L. Wang and G. de Boer.
A transient multiscale framework for elastohydrodynamic lubrication of rough
ball-in-socket bearings. Accepted for publication in Computer Methods in Applied
Mechanics and Engineering.

A fully transient Heterogeneous Multiscale Method for elastohydrodynamic lubrication
in conformal bearings. Microscale simulations of surface roughness provide corrections
to the macroscale flow and load-bearing response, enabling friction and lubrication
to be predicted without resolving the surface geometry throughout the full bearing
simulation. The multiscale model matches a high-resolution deterministic solution
to within 3% in minimum film thickness and 3% in pressure at a thirteenfold reduction
in computational cost, demonstrated under ASTM F3143 reciprocating hip loading and
velocity profiles.
